generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the benefits of learning by doing are clear across any field. A placement or project gives you authentic experience of how the work is really done, not just how it is written up. You build practical skills by using them, you grow in confidence with real tasks and real people, and you begin to see yourself as a future practitioner, which is exactly what employers look for.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students finish the same placement and are asked what they got out of it.

{{learner-a}} says it was fine, but cannot point to anything gained. {{learner-a}} did the tasks without noticing what they taught, and comes away with hours completed but no sense of having developed.

{{learner-b}} can name what the placement gave them: real skills used for the first time, more confidence with people, and a clearer idea of the career they want. {{learner-b}} sees the experience as something that developed them, not just time served.

Both did the same placement. Only {{learner-b}} recognised its benefits: the authentic experience, the skills, the confidence and the sense of direction it offered.
generatedProse.summary: Practice- and work-based learning is valuable because it offers authentic experience of real work, builds practical skills by using them, grows your confidence, and helps you see yourself as a future practitioner. You can now describe these benefits and recognise them in a student's experience. With a clear picture of what this learning is, the forms it takes and why it matters, you are ready to make the most of it when it comes.

check.body: In the worked example, what showed that {{learner-b}} had gained from the placement?

items.text: {{learner-b}} could name real skills, more confidence, and a clearer sense of the career they wanted.
{{learner-b}} said it was fine but could point to nothing.

feedback.correct: That's right. Being able to name skills, confidence and a clearer direction shows the experience developed them.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} could point to as having gained.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} had gained because they could name real skills, more confidence and a clearer sense of the career they wanted.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
